questions.text: What is the safest first distinction in a change-order question?

options.text: A claim or notice is not automatically an approved change order
Every verbal site request is final approval
Only the contractor can decide contract time
The building permit replaces contract documentation

questions.rationale: The written notice path starts the claim; approval still depends on contract authority and documentation.
questions.explanation: Omits critical information; proposals must include work description, specifications, drawings, and schedule impact. Omits cost information; proposals must include both cost and schedule impacts. Contradicts best practice; drawings are essential to communicate the scope change clearly. A complete change order proposal documents the scope change, technical requirements, visual representation, cost estimate, and time impact. Change order proposals must include work description, specifications, drawings, cost estimate, and schedule impact analysis.

questions.text: What does CIAP Document 102 say about emergency work not caused by the contractor?

options.text: It is treated as work under a change order
It is always unpaid volunteer work
It is a building permit amendment only
It is the architect's personal liability

questions.rationale: Emergency work to prevent loss is treated as change-order work unless caused by contractor fault or negligence.

questions.text: What happens when increased quantities or scope result from field adjustments under CIAP Document 102?

options.text: The change is covered by a change order
The contractor absorbs all cost without notice in every case
The architect issues a certificate of occupancy
The payment bond is cancelled

questions.rationale: The source ties increased scope or quantities to change-order coverage.

questions.text: For materially different subsurface conditions requiring additional work, what is source-safe?

options.text: A change order is necessary and issued to the contractor
The owner ignores the condition because it was underground
The architect changes the law by memo
The contractor receives automatic final payment

questions.rationale: CIAP Document 102 requires a change order when different subsurface conditions require additional or different work.
questions.explanation: Overly restrictive; directive changes can increase, decrease, or neutrally affect cost. Contradicts reality; directive changes affect schedule like any other scope modification. Contradicts best practice; directive changes require careful documentation since pricing is finalized later. Directive changes are owner directives for immediate scope modification when final impacts cannot be determined precisely beforehand. Directive changes are owner orders to proceed with modifications before costs are fully determined; final pricing comes later.

questions.text: What is the checked notice period for an extra-cost claim under CIAP Document 102?

options.text: 15 days
5 working days
30 calendar days
One year

questions.rationale: The contractor gives written notice within fifteen days after the relevant instruction or owner-caused delay recognition.

questions.text: What does UAP Document 301 say about the architect's authority during construction?

options.text: The architect acts only to the extent expressly provided in the contract documents or in writing
The architect has unlimited spending authority
The architect replaces the owner in all financial decisions
The architect can waive all contract documents orally

questions.rationale: The architect is the owner's representative only within the authority stated by the contract or writing.

questions.text: What matters does UAP Document 301 place within the architect's decision role?

options.text: Claims, execution, progress, and interpretation of the contract documents
Issuance of government occupancy permits
Tax collection from the contractor
Cancellation of all bonds without owner action

questions.rationale: The checked source assigns contract-administration decisions to the architect within stated limits.
questions.explanation: Omits critical information; schedule impact documentation is essential to prevent disputes. Splits the change order inappropriately; both cost and schedule must be in the change order for complete documentation. Creates risk; owner-directed delays still require formal documentation to protect the contractor from liquidated damages. Change orders must address both cost and schedule; time extensions are formalized to avoid liquidated damages for owner-directed delays. Change orders must quantify schedule impacts and establish revised completion dates to avoid liquidated damages disputes.

questions.text: If the owner accepts defective or nonconforming work instead of requiring correction, what does CIAP Document 102 require where appropriate?

options.text: A change order reflecting a price reduction
Automatic full payment with no adjustment
A new architectural license
A fire safety inspection certificate

questions.rationale: The source uses a change order to reflect a reduction in contract price where appropriate.

questions.text: Which statement best protects the owner and contractor in a change-order dispute?

options.text: Use written notice, source-backed evaluation, owner authority, and a written change order
Let the site conversation stand without records
Ignore the contract and use a generic industry habit
Treat every claim as immediately approved

questions.rationale: The checked sources support a documented contract path, not informal approval.

questions.text: A contractor starts extra work after an owner instruction but gives no timely notice. What is the exam-safe issue?

options.text: Whether the extra-cost claim followed the required written notice path
Whether the architect can issue a tax receipt
Whether the building can be occupied without OBO approval
Whether the payment bond becomes a design fee

questions.rationale: The source-safe issue is the extra-cost notice path and subsequent change-order approval.
